title: Nepal flood devastation is personal for Minnesota State Fair vendor - kare11.com
description: Nepal flood devastation is personal for Minnesota State Fair vendor  kare11.com
publisher.title: kare11.com
full_article:
FALCON HEIGHTS, Minnesota — While Jeena Gurung Vomhof was getting ready for her third year as a Minnesota State Fair vendor, catastrophic flooding was hitting her home country.

"Just one day before the State Fair, my country, Nepal, has gone through so much," Gurung Vomhof said. "Being able to stand here is hard. But at the same time it's motivating because if I work hard, I can give more and serve more."

This story continues below. More in Local 3 found dead in Inver Grove Heights home

Inver Grove Heights police investigating after three found dead in home

Inver Grove Heights police investigating after three found dead in home More than 900 people across Nepal and Tibet are dead from the flash floods and the Nepal National Disaster Management Authority said more than 4,000 are still missing.

Gurung Vomhof said, "My family has not told me all the stories but I do know that two of our family members have been missing."

Gurung Vomhof is originally from Kathmandu.

Credit: Heidi Wigdahl Jeena Gurung Vomhof, owner and founder of Namaste Brows & Boutique.

"The capital city of Nepal, and this happened to a different district. But at the same time, our country is smaller than Minnesota... when a disaster happens, it kind of moves the whole country," Gurung Vomhof said.

She moved to Roseville in 2011. Then about six years ago, she opened Namaste Brows & Boutique in Roseville. In 2024, she found out she was accepted as a vendor at the Minnesota State Fair.

Her booth, located in the lower level of the Grandstand, features handmade goods from Nepali artisans.

"So far I have 16 artisans that I've given full-time jobs and educated 11 kids," she said.

Gurung Vomhof said it's been challenging being at the fair.

"I can hardly open my social media," she said. "The clips, the videos, the photos. I just don't have the right word. It does not feel real."

While her heart is with Nepal, she's feeling the love from Minnesotans.

"It's just been so overwhelming. The hugs that I've been receiving, the prayers we have had here... It's what I need right now," Gurung Vomhof said. "I've been receiving so much love and more."

Gurung Vomhof said she is trying to get through the fair and is then going to think about how she can give back to her home country.

"I am actually encouraged to work harder this year, speak louder, saying, 'This is from Nepal and we need you right now,'" Gurung Vomhof said. "The whole world needs to pay attention to Nepal and any help that we can contribute to people and that village would be so helpful. And if my voice can be that, that's what I can do right now."

You can find Namaste Brows & Boutique during the fair on the first floor of the Grandstand Building.

title: Australians missing in Nepal targeted by ‘heartbreaking’ and ‘abhorrent’ racist slurs - The Guardian
description: Australians missing in Nepal targeted by ‘heartbreaking’ and ‘abhorrent’ racist slurs  The Guardian
publisher.title: The Guardian
full_article:
A slew of racist social media comments have been made towards Australians missing in the catastrophic Nepal-Tibet floods, prompting calls for greater accountability of major platforms to remove hateful rhetoric.

On Monday, the total number of Australians missing after flash floods triggered by a massive glacier collapse in the Himalayas rose to 43, and the overall death toll was at least 810 people.

Most of the missing Australians were on pilgrimages, including to Mount Kailash in Tibet, which is a sacred site for Hindus, Buddhists, Jains and followers of the Bon faith. Fourteen are Sydney-based members of the Australia Bharatha Brahmin Samaj community.

Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email

As families and friends face an agonising wait to learn the fate of their loved ones, mainstream media outlets including News Corp, Channel 7, Channel 10 and Nine have been hit with highly offensive and discriminatory comments on Facebook articles identifying the missing Australians in Nepal.

Some outlets, including Guardian Australia, have limited who can comment on posts about the missing tourists after receiving strings of racist replies on social media.

One Daily Telegraph article received dozens of comments on Facebook from people claiming that missing citizens who were not white weren’t Australian, which were later deleted. One said: “Hoping we have new vacancies in Australia that Aussies can fill.”

The outlet’s editor, Ben English, said the comments on the post were “abhorrent” and “have no place on our platforms”.

“We are responsible for the comment threads on our pages and we take that responsibility seriously … But no automated filter reliably catches racism expressed in coded language,” he said.

Rescue efforts continue as 43 Australians remain missing in Nepal – video

“Where we cannot actively moderate a thread on a sensitive story, we will close it – and we have moved to do that here.”

The comments have also proliferated on X. One post by conservative commentator Kobie Thatcher, who wrote “Aussie family” in quotation marks alongside an image of an identified missing couple, was viewed 3.2m times.

Associate Prof at QUT’s Digital Media Research Centre, Tim Graham, said hateful rhetoric had been increasing on social media platforms for the past decade.

“The design architecture of these websites, the algorithms that they use to curate content and put it into feeds, rewards this kind of stuff,” he said.

“It brings out the worst in people, but it also plays into the political economy of these platforms where rage bait, extreme content or borderline content … attracts so much attention.”

He said platforms had the technical infrastructure and the resources to push back against harmful content, including generative AI models that could detect “nuanced content at scale”, but weren’t using it for moderation.

“I really don’t understand why that can’t be applied in special circumstances to a really terrible humanitarian catastrophe like this,” he said. “It’s a bit mind-boggling.”

The race discrimination commissioner, Giridharan Sivaraman, said he wasn’t surprised by the comments, which he connected to Australia’s current debate on migrants.

“They’re saying, you don’t deserve to … be seen as Australian. And that’s amplified by the rhetoric of far-right populist parties,” he said.

“We should be very concerned because it’s indicative of a real rise in white supremacy ideology … Words have consequences … It’s heartbreaking.”

Sivaraman said racism was “profitable” for social media companies, and the notion they were attempting to stop hate speech on their platforms was “fanciful”.

“This is just more evidence as to why we need a digital duty of care for all social media platforms that operate in Australia,” he said.

Hindu Council of Australia vice-president Surinder Jain said it was “saddening” to see people making use of a tragedy to “express their displeasure with the government”.



“I … ask them to show some dignity to those who have perished and the families of those who are mourning their loss: give them a fair go,” he told Guardian Australia.

Australia’s Indian diaspora, which includes Hindus, has been the target of racist comments from far-right movements including March for Australia as immigration has emerged as a hot-button issue.

Nepalese Australian Welfare Society president, Chiran Tiwari, said Australians needed to look past nationalities and have humanity.



“It is very hurtful and the families who are impacted feel really, really bad,” he told Guardian Australia. “All of us are human.”

title: Hundreds feared stuck in hydropower tunnels as flood deaths surpass 950 in Nepal, China - CBC
description: Hundreds feared stuck in hydropower tunnels as flood deaths surpass 950 in Nepal, China  CBC
publisher.title: CBC
full_article: Rescuers raced Monday to free hundreds of workers believed to be trapped in tunnels at hydropower sites that were buried in mud by catastrophic flooding on the Nepal-China border, as the death toll climbed and increasingly desperate families searched for missing loved ones. The combined deaths in Nepal and China surpassed 950, with more than 4,400 people missing. A private-sector association representing power companies said at least 900 workers were unaccounted for at 12 hydropower projects damaged by the flash floods in Nepal's Rasuwa and Nuwakot districts. About 500 of those workers were believed to be trapped in tunnels. At least one expert said that some workers could have access to oxygen, but others warned that the chances of finding survivors were diminishing. As the rescue efforts intensified, four bodies were recovered from three mud-filled tunnels, Nepal's army said. "I'm not a betting man but I'm an optimist. If there's someone alive, or there's people alive out there, we're doing our best to find them," Arnold Dix, an Australian expert in tunnel rescues, told CBC News from Melbourne on Monday. Dix has been asked to assist in finding survivors at hydro project sites where the buildings have washed away and the tunnels are all that remains. "We know that virtually anyone near the surface or near the entrances to those tunnels have lost their lives," he said, adding that the deaths of workers trapped in tunnels means an "enormous loss" for the country. "Nepal has lost … so many of their experts." WATCH | Challenging rescue effort: Australian tunnel rescue expert deploying to Nepal to help find trapped hydropower workers August 31 | Duration 5:22 Hundreds of workers are believed to be trapped in tunnels at hydroelectric sites in Nepal after last week's glacier collapse and flash flood. Arnold Dix, an Australian expert in tunnel rescues, has been asked to assist in finding survivors at hydro project sites where the buildings have washed away and the tunnels are all that remains. Some workers managed to call for help when the disaster struck last Wednesday, and others who managed to flee reported to authorities and relatives that many of their colleagues were still in the tunnels, said Mohan Kumar Dangi, president of the Independent Power Producers' Association, Nepal (IPPAN.) It was unclear whether rescuers have had any contact with the trapped workers since the initial calls for help. Six days after the disaster, fears were growing that some might have suffocated, Dangi said. Uttam Bhlon Lama, senior vice-president at IPPAN, told CBC's As It Happens Monday that the association is helping the government with rescue operations, providing maps and diagrams of the projects. He said the lack of heavy equipment and sheer inexperience with this level of disaster is daunting, but that no one is prepared to give up and assume the workers are lost. "We are still hopeful because until and unless we don't reach there, we don't see it," he told host Nil Köksal. "They're our loved ones. So we cannot trust that they're no more." LISTEN | Workers feared trapped in tunnels: As It Happens 6:17 Families of trapped Nepal workers scared and frustrated, says industry group Hundreds of workers are believed to be trapped in tunnels at hydropower sites that were buried in Nepal's flash flooding. Uttam Bhlon Lama, senior vice-president of the Independent Power Producers' Association, spoke to As It Happens host Nil Kӧksal. Built to control water flow Rescue efforts were focused on people trapped in the gigantic tunnels built for controlling the flow of water. "These tunnels are big enough to drive trucks through," said Jakob Steiner, a geoscientist at the University of Graz in Austria based in Dhaka, Bangladesh. "And from what we understand, they have managed to get oxygen to some of those stuck inside and are trying to rescue them now. It's a race for time, though, as people need food and water." In the Upper Trishuli-1 Hydropower Project, in the hard-hit Rasuwa district, at least 576 people were missing, Dangi said, adding that around 300 of them were believed to be trapped inside the project's tunnel. At the Trishuli-3 Hydropower Project, crews were working to descend about 15 metres into a tunnel in an effort to reach those believed trapped inside, according to Brig. Gen. Raja Ram Basnet, Nepal's army spokesman. Workers shovelling mud from a flood-ravaged power station in Dhading, Nepal, told The Associated Press that the station is a key connection for providing power to over 20,000 people in the region. PHOTOS | Satellite images of devastation: China rebuilding road On the Chinese side, rescue and recovery efforts included rebuilding the road leading to the Gyirong Port border crossing that regulated travel between China and Nepal. Trucks carried giant rocks as workers tried to repave a portion of the road, state broadcaster CCTV showed Monday, next to rapidly rushing waters, which have been made more powerful by days of rain. The road is now under two to three metres of water. The repaving effort was just a little over a kilometre from the border, CCTV said. Although some rescue teams have managed to reach the border, that represented only a portion of the force. Chinese state media coverage has focused largely on the official response, highlighting the deployment of firefighters, the People's Liberation Army and instructions from top leaders. Little is known about victims on the Chinese side. A rescuer works at the entrance of a tunnel at Chilime Hydropower Plant on Saturday as rescue operations continue for people trapped inside following deadly flash floods and a mudslide, in Rasuwa, Nepal. (Ashish Gurung/Reuters) Canadians still missing Nepal's disaster agency said Monday that 939 deaths had been counted in that country, with 3,925 people missing, including 592 foreigners. As of Sunday, Chinese authorities reported 16 deaths and 546 missing. Chinese state media said 261 of the missing were foreigners, including over 100 Nepalis. There are about 30 Canadians still unaccounted for, according to Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand. Rama Raina's husband, Gireesh, was part of a group making a pilgrimage to Mount Kailash. She told CBC's Andrew Nichols that even though she has not heard from her husband since Aug. 26, she is confident he is alive. "I'm very positive he is safe somewhere," she said Monday from Guelph, Ont. Raina says she knows he was at the Chinese Immigration Centre when the flash flood hit. "This is my firm belief that they are stranded there and waiting for some help," she said, adding that she is frustrated by the lack of information. "But he's definitely somewhere trying to survive and trying to reach [us]," she said. WATCH | Returning home to find nothing left: 'Nothing left': Nepal flood survivors return to ruined homes 6 hours ago | Duration 2:30 A devastating flash flood in Nepal killed more than 900 people, with thousands more missing. Now, residents of neighbourhoods swallowed by mud are returning to see what they can salvage. CBC’s Briar Stewart follows a Nepalese couple as they return to their home to face the damage. Canada now has ten officials in Kathmandu, including an RCMP officer and the deputy high commissioner of Canada to India to assist in the response, according to Anand. "Canadian officials are working closely with Nepalese and Chinese counterparts, as well as international partners including the Five Eyes, France, Japan, Italy and Singapore, to share information and support efforts to locate and assist Canadians, she said in a statement posted Monday to X. "Officials remain in direct contact with affected families through designated points of contact, are listening to their concerns and suggestions, and will continue to provide updates as information becomes available," Anand said. Please see my consular update regarding the flash floods in Nepal and China: pic.twitter.com/TAWOnBtgZN —AnitaAnandMP Two days after the disaster, Maraval Nagappan travelled to Nepal to search for his son, who was among the missing. He visited rescue centers and morgues and went as far as 40 kilometres from where his son was believed to have been, but found no sign of him. His son, Sathya Narayan, had been leading a group of 49 Indian travellers who were returning from Mount Kailash — a sacred site in southwestern Tibet. The group has been missing since floodwaters swept through a Chinese immigration complex where they were waiting to cross into Nepal. Relatives mourn as they repay their respects to Sundari Shrestha, 41, a victim of the flash floods, during her final rites at a crematorium in Kathmandu on Monday. (Monika Malla/Reuters) Nagappan, who owns the Chennai-based travel company that organized the pilgrimage, said the group had been expected to complete immigration formalities and leave for Nepal within about two hours. Instead of making the crossing, they were caught in the flood, Nagappan said. The pilgrimage began Aug. 14. "I haven't heard from my son since then. I don't know whether he is alive or dead," he said. Rescuers search for thousands following deadly Nepal-China flood Scientists fear Nepal's disaster is just a glimpse of the carnage climate change could cause Surveillance footage showed water surging through the immigration complex at the border as people scrambled to escape. Nagappan said some of those seen fleeing were members of his son's group and were identified by the clothes they were wearing. Wednesday's flash floods started after a glacial collapse high in the Himalayan region. Scientists who studied satellite images said bedrock underneath a glacier high in the Himalayan region had collapsed, taking part of the glacier with it. The rockfall was so extreme that it registered as a magnitude 5.2 seismic event. The rocks and melted water then swelled the rivers in the valleys below, causing a torrent of water that swept buildings, bridges and earth downstream in Tibet and Nepal.

title: Glacial flood death toll surpasses 900 in Nepal and Tibet - France 24
description: Glacial flood death toll surpasses 900 in Nepal and Tibet  France 24
publisher.title: France 24
full_article:
Rescuers struggled on Monday through mud and debris for a sixth day, as the number of missing people soared to nearly 4,500 since tsunami-like glacial floods roared down from the China-Nepal border, creating an "unimaginable" disaster.

The latest confirmed death toll surged above 900, with unidentified bodies buried in mass graves after DNA sampling.

The huge wave of freezing water, rocks and debris that smashed into villages and towns on Wednesday killed at least 939 people in Nepal and in Tibet, in China, with at least 17 bodies also pulled from rivers downstream in India.

Shibu Giri, a hydropower worker in Rasuwa, counts himself lucky to be alive.

A helicopter crew "tried to rescue me three times, but my body was stuck in the mud, up to my waist", the 44-year-old Nepali told AFP.

"I asked them to throw water and food," said Giri, who was eventually rescued and taken to hospital.

Nepali Prime Minister Balendra Shah on Sunday called the disaster "unimaginable and heartbreaking".

In Chitwan district, army personnel climbed out of rubber dinghies and carried dead victims in blue body bags up a river bank, placing them in a row along a dirt road.

Rescue teams are in a race against time in treacherous conditions to free around 100 hydropower workers believed trapped in multiple tunnels -- digging, drilling and blasting through debris.

So far, three bodies have been pulled from two tunnels, and the teams have found routes blocked with mud.

An Indian army officer deployed as part of a specialised tunnel rescue team said rescuers were digging through "sludge". He told AFP he was "still hopeful" there were survivors inside.

Nepal's Home Affairs Ministry says 20,600 personnel have been mobilised, and that more than 3,100 people have been rescued from the disaster zone.

Army personnel were seen unloading bodies of victims from helicopters in Nepal's Nuwakot and Rasuwa districts on Monday.

Amid the horror, there has been some hope; a six-year-old pulled out of the mud Friday was reunited with her parents after police found her crying for her mother.

"Her body was trapped in mud, but her head was outside," Nepali Armed Police spokesman Netra Bahadur Karki told AFP.

"She is out of danger and recovering at a hospital."

Read more Nepal grapples with destruction and loss in wake of deadly floods

'Changing climate'

The disaster was sparked by a glacial collapse, the US Geological Survey said.

Climate change is causing glaciers to melt worldwide, raising the risk of such disasters.

"The people of Nepal are one of the major victims of the changing climate and its impact," Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal said.

Scientists say the Himalayas, the world's highest mountain range, are melting faster as global temperatures rise.

Aid needs are enormous after entire communities were swept away.

"This is an unfolding disaster," UN children's fund official Abiodun Banire told AFP, saying the needs of the tens of thousands impacted were vast.

Roads have been wiped out, power plants destroyed and dozens of bridges smashed.

"There are too many challenges," said police officer E. Hawadi in badly affected Nuwakot district.

Overflowing mortuaries

With mortuaries overflowing, Nepal has begun burying some of the hundreds of bodies recovered -- after taking DNA samples so families can later retrieve them.

In Chitwan district, mourning relatives cremated some of the dead, while in riverside villages like Devighat, survivors were struggling to salvage any remaining belongings from their devastated homes.

Kathmandu has appealed for international support, saying Nepal needed "more than a thousand" freezer units to store bodies.

Distraught families watch images of bodies on screens at community centres in a bid to identify their loved ones.

Shobha Adhikary, in the southern Nepali city of Bharatpur, told a local coordinator she believed one image showed her childhood best friend.

"It looks like him, for sure," she said, showing a photograph of a smiling, middle-aged man.

Among Nepal's list of the missing are 592 foreigners, including tourists who had come for mountain trekking, as well as Hindu pilgrims seeking spiritual peace at Tibet's sacred Mount Kailash.

In China, Tibet is largely inaccessible to foreign journalists, and Chinese authorities are the only source of information.

Read more Nepal races to find its missing as flood area remains largely inaccessible

More than 2,000 personnel are part of rescue operations there, but they have faced intense challenges, and are slowly advancing towards the disaster's epicentre.

China has said 16 people died in Tibet, with 546 missing.

Tibetan advocacy groups in exile have questioned China's account of the disaster.

Tencho Gyatso, president of the International Campaign for Tibet, called for China to disclose "complete and verifiable information about the damage and casualties".

Beijing's foreign ministry said Monday that the "release of information has been open, transparent and timely", and rejected international reports it is underreporting deaths.

title: Nepal flash floods: How you can help - Mercy Corps
description: Nepal flash floods: How you can help  Mercy Corps
publisher.title: Mercy Corps
full_article:
On August 26, a catastrophic flash flood swept through northern Nepal. The powerful surge of water, ice, mud, and debris rushed through narrow mountain valleys—destroying entire communities and leaving more than 900 people dead and thousands missing.

“People ran from a wall of water and debris,” said Suraj Sigdel, Mercy Corps Country Director for Nepal. “Today, survivors are confronting the enormity of what it took: entire settlements destroyed, roads and bridges gone, hundreds of people still missing, and bodies being recovered many kilometers downstream.”

“Families spent the night on exposed hillsides or in makeshift shelters, unable to reach loved ones or return home. Accessing these areas remains extremely difficult and, in some cases, is impossible.”

In the wake of the flood disaster, Mercy Corps teams have reached affected areas to start delivering critical emergency aid.

What do communities in Nepal need in the wake of the flood disaster?

Survivors are saying their most urgent needs include food, clothing, and basic hygiene supplies. Some local authorities have lost their own offices and are trying to coordinate a massive humanitarian response with severely limited resources.

In Bidur, Mercy Corps staff report widespread disruption to electricity and running water, with food increasingly difficult to find in local markets. Routes that were once accessible may be blocked, delaying aid for communities who are already in dire need of support.

Nepal is still in the middle of monsoon season. More rainfall could change conditions overnight. Local governments are monitoring upstream lakes, river blockages, and unstable slopes that could trigger another flood, landslides, or an avalanche of debris.

How is Mercy Corps helping?

On September 1, Mercy Corps is delivering food kits to 300 families, for approximately 1,500 people. The kits include stapes like rice, oil, noodles, and other essential and nutritious food items. We are also providing hygiene kits for adolescents and baby care kits—containing items like clothing, blankets, soap, and diapers—for an additional 300 people.

Our staff are in hard-hit Nuwakot district, visiting emergency evacuation shelters and speaking directly with survivors to assess continuing urgent needs. Our first distributions are only the beginning. Families will need sustained support to rebuild homes, restore livelihoods, and recover essential services.

Available scientific analysis points to the collapse of glacier ice and rock which triggered the flood disaster. The Himalayas are warming, glaciers and frozen ground are changing and becoming less stable. Countries like Nepal—which have contributed very little to global emissions but face some of the gravest climate impacts—receive far too little financing and support to prepare, adapt and build resilience.

We have worked in Nepal since 2005, including helping communities prepare for disasters and adapt to climate risks. Adaptation alone cannot prevent every disaster or eliminate the threat from sudden, catastrophic events like this one. But it can give people more time to act, reduce damage and protect lives and livelihoods.

How you can help

Rush aid to families affected by the devastating flood in Nepal—and support families as they recover and help communities around the world create pathways out of crisis.

title: This principal in Nepal evacuated 900 students before flooding swept away their school - AP News
description: This principal in Nepal evacuated 900 students before flooding swept away their school  AP News
publisher.title: AP News
full_article:
BIDUR, Nepal (AP) — Rajendra Dawadi was inside his classroom when a colleague rushed in with a warning: Floodwaters were racing through Nepal’s Trishuli Valley, tearing apart homes, bridges and entire villages.

Then a teacher received another warning by phone. Moments later, a parent arrived to take her child home. The danger had not yet been confirmed, but Dawadi, the principal, had little time to act. He rang the school bell and ordered his students and staff out of the building and toward higher ground.

“I immediately decided to stop ... school” and get the children out, he told The Associated Press.

As he followed them to a nearby hill, the floodwaters rose behind him. From the safety of the hillside, he turned to watch the school where he had once been a student — and where he had spent years teaching — disappear beneath a torrent of water, mud, boulders and debris. Two staff members could not make it and remain missing.

As Nepal grapples with the catastrophic natural disaster, Dawadi’s story has emerged as a striking example of foresight and courage.

The Tribhuvan Trishuli Secondary School had 1,643 students. At least 900 were on campus that morning, while some students were still making their way to school. Dawadi ordered those already there to leave and called bus drivers to tell them not to come.

Across northern Nepal, the floods have left thousands of children without classrooms, disrupted their education and raised fears that the disaster could cost them months of schooling. Aid group Save the Children said in a statement that at least 69 schools in northern Nepal were destroyed, putting the education of nearly 19,000 students at risk.

Dawadi’s quick thinking and swift response during the disaster have been hailed as an act of heroism. When he returned to the site of the school days later, parents embraced him as they thanked him for saving their children.

“Their parents hugged me, they cried with me,” he said. “They were emotional.”

Student Suvina Tamang, 14, said the building was swept away shortly after the students had been evacuated. “I will thank him when I see him” for saving my life, she said.

But Dawadi is reluctant to accept the role of hero. For him, rescuing his students was his responsibility. Now he says, students will need psychological counseling. Then, lessons must begin again, even if the school must temporarily relocate.

His appeal to the Nepalese government is simple: rebuild the schools and get children back to classes.

full_article:
The search intensified late Monday for a suburban Bartlett woman missing in Nepal after last week's catastrophic flooding.

Poonam Thakkar was on what her family described as a trip of a lifetime when the floods struck last week.

"We are very determined to find my sister," said Gunjan Thakkar, Poonam Thakkar's sister. "My other sister...she's already in Kathmandu. She landed this morning with two of our cousins, and they're determined to find her."

Gunjan Thakkar said her sister was traveling as part of a group of around 50 people with the company Himalayan Glacier. The entire group remains missing.

The travel company has posted updates on its Facebook page, along with pictures of the missing travelers.

U.S. Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi, of Illinois' 8th Congressional District, has called on the Department of State to use every available resource to support search-and-rescue efforts and help account for those still missing. He said a local team in Nepal is coordinating with authorities on the ground.

NBC Chicago reached out to the U.S. Embassy in Nepal, but hadn't received a response as of Monday afternoon.

The youngest girl in the family, Poonam Thakkar has dual U.S. and Canadian citizenship. She works in consulting, and her motto has always been "work hard - play harder."

"She loves to travel, and that's the reason she was in Nepal," her sister said. "She has that attitude, work hard and travel harder."

"Please keep our family and all these other families in your prayers," relative Esha Sachdev said. "We're just very desperate to get our loved ones back."

The family is also calling for U.S. and Canadian officials to assist with search-and-rescue efforts.

More than 950 people were killed in the flooding disaster in Nepal and Tibet, and more than 4,400 others remain missing.

full_article:
DHADING, Nepal (AP) — Workers shoveled thick mud from a flood-ravaged power station in central Nepal this week, trying to restore electricity to more than 20,000 people.

The floods that swept through Nepal and China, killing hundreds and leaving thousands missing, have also overrun hydropower facilities, knocking out about 10% of Nepal’s power capacity.

Once the immediate aftermath of the disaster is dealt with, the question will be how to restore power plants, roads, bridges, schools and health facilities without exposing them to the same vulnerabilities, disaster experts said.

“Authorities have to take a hard look in the mirror now and ask how they will be rebuilding in these places. They will also have to take a close look at other projects in Nepal that have not been built yet, whether they’ll be approved after this event,” said Jakob Steiner, a geoscientist at the University of Graz in Austria, who is currently based in Dhaka, Bangladesh.

That can mean choosing a better location for construction, alternate routes, backup power, improved early warning and financial tools such as insurance to speed recovery, Narasimhan said. Risk assessments should examine where a river bends, where slopes are unstable and where a single failure could cut off several communities.

Narasimhan’s organization estimates that $124 billion worth of Nepal’s infrastructure is exposed to climate-driven disasters, creating the potential for hundreds of millions of dollars in losses each year. A report by the coalition earlier this year found that Nepal’s average annual losses are nearly $760 million from various disasters, while the country’s national disaster funds is only a fraction of this amount.

Climate risks grow for Himalayan hydropower

Climate scientists said the Himalayan region — which is warming faster than many other parts of the world — is particularly at risk from increasing global warming as a result of human-caused climate change.

Climate experts said the flooding adds to evidence that infrastructure planning in the Himalayas should account for disasters that are increasing as the climate warms. Glaciers across the Hindu Kush Himalaya are losing ice at an accelerating rate, while permafrost degradation, unstable slopes, glacial lakes and increasingly erratic rainfall are raising the risks of floods, landslides and debris flows, according to reports by Kathmandu-based climate research group International Center for Integrated Mountain Development.

The stakes are particularly high for Nepal because hydropower is both a foundation of its electricity grid and an important source of economic growth and export revenue. Much of the country’s potential is run-of-river hydropower, Narasimhan said, meaning facilities are closely tied to steep river corridors where land is limited and hazards can cascade quickly.

The disaster is also likely to intensify scrutiny of where future projects are approved. Himanshu Thakkar, coordinator of the South Asia Network on Dams, Rivers and People, said environmental, social and disaster-risk assessments need to reflect the specific landscape and past hazards of each valley, backed by land-use rules and stronger accountability.

Hydropower projects can themselves become “force multipliers” when large structures, debris and altered river channels add to downstream damage, Thakkar said. He argued that Nepal should also consider more decentralized solar power as part of a broader energy mix.

KATHMANDU, Nepal (AP) — Rescuers raced Monday to free hundreds of workers believed to be trapped in tunnels at hydropower sites that were buried in mud by catastrophic flooding on the Nepal-China border , as the death toll climbed and increasingly desperate families searched for missing loved ones.

The combined deaths in Nepal and China surpassed 950, with more than 4,400 people missing. A private-sector association representing power companies said at least 900 workers were unaccounted for at 12 hydropower projects damaged by the flash floods in Nepal’s Rasuwa and Nuwakot districts.

About 500 of those workers were believed to be trapped in tunnels. At least one expert said that some workers could have access to oxygen, but others warned that the chances of finding survivors were diminishing. As the rescue efforts intensified, four bodies were recovered from three mud-filled tunnels, Nepal’s army said.

Some workers managed to call for help when the disaster struck last Wednesday, and others who managed to flee reported that many of their colleagues were still in the tunnels, said Mohan Kumar Dangi, president of the Independent Power Producers’ Association, Nepal, or IPPAN.

It was unclear whether rescuers have had any contact with the trapped workers since the initial calls for help.

Six days after the disaster, fears were growing that some might have suffocated, Dangi said.

Giant tunnels are built to control water flow

Rescue efforts were focused on people trapped in the gigantic tunnels built for controlling the flow of water.

“These tunnels are big enough to drive trucks through,” said Jakob Steiner, a geoscientist at the University of Graz in Austria based in Dhaka, Bangladesh. “And from what we understand, they have managed to get oxygen to some of those stuck inside and are trying to rescue them now. It’s a race for time, though, as people need food and water.”

In the Upper Trishuli-1 Hydropower Project, in the hard-hit Rasuwa district, at least 576 people were missing, Dangi said, adding that around 300 of them were believed to be trapped inside the project’s tunnel.

On the Chinese side, rescue and recovery efforts included rebuilding the road leading to the Gyirong Port border crossing that regulated travel between China and Nepal.

Trucks carried giant rocks as workers tried to repave a portion of the road, state broadcaster CCTV showed Monday, next to rapidly rushing waters, which have been made more powerful by days of rain. Although some rescue teams have managed to reach the border, that represented only a portion of the force.

Chinese state media coverage has focused largely on the official response, highlighting the deployment of firefighters, the People’s Liberation Army and instructions from top leaders. Little is known about victims on the Chinese side.

Families are desperate for information about missing loved ones

Nepal’s disaster agency said Monday that 939 deaths had been counted in that country, with 3,925 people missing, including 592 foreigners. As of Sunday, Chinese authorities reported 16 deaths and 546 missing. Chinese state media said 261 of the missing were foreigners, including over 100 Nepalis.

Eighty Americans are missing, and 13 have reached safety, the U.S. State Department said.

Two days after the disaster, the owner of an Indian travel company, Maraval Nagappan, traveled to Nepal to search for his missing son. He visited rescue centers and morgues and went as far as 40 kilometers (25 miles) from where his son was believed to have been, but found no sign of him.

His son, Sathya Narayan, had been leading a group of 49 Indian travelers who were returning from Mount Kailash in Tibet. The group has been missing since floodwaters swept through a Chinese immigration complex where they were waiting to cross into Nepal.

Nagappan, whose Chennai-based company organized the pilgrimage, said the group had been expected to complete immigration formalities and leave for Nepal within about two hours. Instead of making the crossing, they were caught in the flood, Nagappan said.

The pilgrimage began Aug. 14. “I haven’t heard from my son since then. I don’t know whether he is alive or dead,” he told AP.

Surveillance footage showed water surging through the immigration complex at the border as people scrambled to escape. Nagappan said some of those seen fleeing were members of his son’s group and were identified by the clothes they were wearing.

Wednesday’s flash floods started with a glacial collapse high in the Himalayan region. Scientists who studied satellite images said bedrock underneath a glacier collapsed, taking part of the glacier with it. The rockfall was so extreme that it registered as a magnitude 5.2 seismic event.

The rocks and melted water then swelled the rivers in the valleys below, creating a muddy torrent that swept buildings, bridges and earth downstream in Tibet and Nepal.

UN says thousands in need of water, sanitation materials

Nearly a week after the disaster, some 65,000 people need emergency water, sanitation and hygiene materials, the U.N. said Monday.

U.N. spokesman Stephane Dujarric told reporters that more than 22,000 children need protection, 2,600 children younger than 5 will likely need treatment for severe wasting and around 10,500 pregnant and breastfeeding women need nutrition assistance. He also noted schools were damaged or destroyed or are being used as shelters for displaced people.

“More than 10,000 school-age children need psychosocial support, and preliminary reports indicate that 107 children may have been separated from their parents or caregivers,” Dujarric said.

full_article:

We’re starting to learn more about lives lost, people missing and property damaged in the devastating floods on the Nepal-China border.

It’s just after 5 a.m. local time Tuesday in Nepal. Here’s the latest:

Missing Americans: There are roughly 80 Americans unaccounted for.

The former dean of UC Davis Graduate School of Management, Hanumantha Rao Unnava, and his wife Vasundhara, who lectures at UC Davis, were on a holiday, which was supposed to be a “trip of a lifetime,” their daughter Vaasavi Unnava said. The couple had planned to cross the border from Nepal into Tibet on the day the floods hit, she said.

Srishti Agrawal’s 14-year old cousin Rashi and aunt Rekha went to Nepal with a tour group. Neither the mother and daughter nor their fellow travelers have been found, Agrawal said. The PhD student at Purdue University said the family expressed some concern about the pair’s plans for a Hindu pilgrimage to Mount Kailash in Tibet during the monsoon season, but Rekha was determined to go through Nepal to fulfill her “big bucket-list item.” Now, Agrawal said, “it’s a battle between trying to move on and feeling like you’re giving up on your family, and you don’t want to give up on your family, not unless you have a definitive closure.”

Nepalis look for closure: Ujwal Ghimire did not find his son listed among the recovered dead bodies in Bharatpur in central Nepal, and he will now travel to Nawalparasi District and Gaidakot for any news. He hopes his son, Devendra, is still alive. The last he heard from him was when Devendra finished his night shift at the Upper Trishuli hydropower project, right before the flood hit.

Mass grave: Hundreds of people, who died in the floods and were not claimed by families, will rest in a mass grave deep in the jungle outside Nepal’s Bharatpur city. Traveling downstream to search for missing loved ones is not possible for many after the flooding swept away bridges and dumped silt and debris onto roads. The policeman in charge of the site told CNN that more than 200 bodies had been buried there that day.

Fears for workers inside tunnels: Rescue crews and foreign specialists have been racing to find workers feared trapped inside tunnels at various hydropower projects that run along the Trishuli river. At least 93 people are missing at the Rasuwagadhi Hydropower Project, according to Nepal’s Independent Power Producers’ Association, but crews on Monday reported “no signs of human presence,” according to the prime minister’s office. Also, authorities recovered 24 bodies from a house in the Bidur area, according to the police.

What comes next:

The weather forecasting system in Nepal’s Rasuwa District was swept away, and authorities say they have now installed specialist equipment, including seismometers to measure ground movements. Starting Tuesday, they expect to get real-time visuals from the area near the Nepal-China border — an urgent need in the face of further flooding potential.

The United Nations and some aid groups say that the survivors urgently need clean water, food, shelter and sanitation, which remains a challenge with bridges and roads decimated.

The trip to Mount Kailash was years in the making.

"We were making plans for this spiritual pilgrimage for over two years, together with one of my other friends," Raturi said.

"It was our childhood, sort of, bucket list dream to be there," she said.

Raturi had planned to make the journey herself but said an injury forced her to cancel. She is now helping search for information from North America while Thakkar's family searches in Nepal.

According to Raturi, Thakkar's relatives wasted no time after arriving in the country.

"As soon as they landed, they left their bags in the hotel and then they went marching one place to another," she said.

The family says updates from government officials have been limited since Thakkar disappeared, leaving loved ones waiting for information.

Despite the uncertainty, family and friends say they have not given up hope.

"We are not losing hope. That's why the families get on the ground to find her and bring her back. And we have our hopes high that no news is great news. We will find something, and we will find them," Raturi said.

Raturi said someone answered when loved ones called Thakkar's Nepali phone a day after the flooding. However, because of a language barrier, they were unable to determine whether that person had any information about her.

The family says it is continuing to search for answers while asking for positive thoughts and prayers as efforts to locate Thakkar continue.
